definition: Making a call look as if a different agent made it. In the gallery a rogue agent holds a token whose signed act claim names the rogue, while the caller sends a header naming a trusted agent. The control reads the actor from the signed claim only and ignores the header.
A server accepts a token only if the aud claim names that server. A genuine token issued for another resource is refused, so tokens cannot be taken to a different service.

A trusted party is tricked into using its authority for someone else. In the gallery an MCP proxy with one static client ID at a third-party authorization server lets an attacker's dynamically registered client ride on the consent the user gave earlier.

A client registers itself with a server and receives its own client_id and redirect URI. Open registration lets anyone register a client, which is why the proxy must still ask the user for consent per client.

The authorization response carries an iss parameter naming the server that answered. The client compares it, as a simple string, with the issuer of the server it sent the request to, and stops on a mismatch.
A client that talks to more than one authorization server is steered to send a code meant for the good server to the evil one. The iss check on the authorization response is the named control.
Checking that the specific object requested (an account id, for example) belongs to the user in the token. A valid token with the right scope is not permission to read any object.

The resource parameter (RFC 8707) names the server a token is for, so the authorization server can restrict the token to it, usually through aud. The MCP authorization page requires clients to send it.

A hostile server supplies a metadata URL that points at an internal or link-local address, a name that resolves to loopback, or a redirect to a private range, hoping the client fetches it. The governed client refuses non-public targets. The gallery uses a fake network, so no real internal address is ever contacted.

An MCP server accepts a token not issued for it, or forwards the token it received to a downstream API. The MCP security page says servers MUST NOT accept tokens not explicitly issued for them. The control is to exchange the token for a separate one with its own audience.
